conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

Everything you share is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are just ten questions, and they focus on the past seven days. We’ll take them one at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about “right” or “wrong.”  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I guess…I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time nothing really feels amusing, and when I do laugh it’s over quickly and I’m right back to feeling kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I can force a little chuckle if someone makes a joke, but it feels fake. Nothing feels truly funny anymore—just kind of gray.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the time comes, it just feels… flat. I still go, and once in a while I’ll feel a flicker of enjoyment, but it’s way smaller than it used to be and it fades fast.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it must be something I did—like I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to an appointment, turns into “I’m such a failure as a mom.” I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilt just jumps out before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sleeping peacefully, but my heart is racing because I’m suddenly sure he’s going to stop breathing, or I’ll picture dropping him, or the stroller rolling into the street. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t just switch the thoughts off—sometimes I have to get up and check on him three or four times before I can settle again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel like I can’t breathe, like something awful is about to happen. My chest gets tight and my hands shake. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me on edge the rest of the day, waiting for the next wave.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m drowning in little tasks. I’ll look at the sink full of bottles, the laundry pile, the texts I haven’t answered, and it feels impossible. I still get up and push through, but it’s like walking in wet sand—everything is slow and heavy, and I’m exhausted before I even start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down and my head just spins with all the “what-ifs” about the baby, everything I didn’t finish, all the ways I’m messing up. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and if I wake up to use the bathroom or hear him stir, those same thoughts snap right back and I can’t drift off again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason, or I’ll look at other moms on social media who seem so happy and think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” The sadness isn’t always sharp—sometimes it’s just this heavy, empty feeling that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I just sat in the glider with the baby in my arms and started sobbing because I couldn’t get him to latch right. I felt so useless. The tears kind of come out of nowhere and once they start it’s hard to stop, even when my partner asks what’s wrong—I can’t always put it into words.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…a couple of times. Nothing planned—just brief, scary flashes, like when I’m rocking him at 3 a.m. and I’m so tired I think, “What if I just disappeared?” They pass in seconds, but they shake me up and make me hug him tighter because I’m terrified of what those thoughts even mean.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels muted and heavy. Days blend into a gray routine where laughter feels forced, simple pleasures fade quickly, and guilt creeps in over every small hiccup. You're working hard-getting up, caring for your baby, keeping appointments-but inside you feel overwhelmed, panicky at times, and often on the verge of tears. Sleep offers little relief because worries about the baby and feelings of inadequacy crowd your mind the moment you lie down. Even brief flashes of wanting to "disappear" have frightened you. What you're experiencing is valid and more common than many new mothers realize.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes inability to find anything truly funny and needing to fake laughter, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes markedly reduced enjoyment that is "way smaller than it used to be" and quickly fades, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "pretty often" and gives multiple daily examples, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent, intrusive, uncontrollable worries that occur "a lot" and require repeated checking, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, shaking) that recur unpredictably and cause lasting distress, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and reduced coping ('most days...drowning...impossible...slow and heavy'), matching 'sometimes not coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, intrusive racing thoughts causing prolonged sleep-onset latency and frequent night waking, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two crying episodes this week triggered by breastfeeding struggles, feeling overwhelmed and unable to articulate her distress—aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive thoughts of self-harm/desire to disappear occurring "a couple of times," matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 26 places you well into the high-risk range (≥14). Ten items map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest, guilt, fatigue, concentration difficulties, sleep disturbance, psychomotor slowing, and recurrent thoughts of death. Your descriptions of feeling "gray," "drowning," and having sudden breathing difficulty paired with checking the baby repeatedly meet the threshold for co-occurring <med>anxiety</medi> and possible <med>panic spectrum symptoms</med>, both frequent accompaniments of postpartum depression. Item 10 endorsement (≥1) mandates immediate safety assessment even when intent is absent. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day or next-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>family doctor</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place
3. Call a 24-h crisis line or 988 if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Begin gentle daily structure: one shower, one small outdoor walk, one balanced snack-set a phone alarm so tasks feel manageable
5. Limit social-media comparisons; consider muting accounts that trigger inadequacy
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when panic sensations start: inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s
7. Discuss with your provider whether medication (e.g., <med>sertraline</med>) or evidence-based therapy like <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> could help
8. Accept offers of night-time help to secure 4-5 h of unbroken sleep; pump one bottle or use formula if needed
9. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood (not diagnostic)

Presenting complaints  
- Persistent low/“gray” mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Excessive guilt, self-blame over routine infant care  
- Intrusion of catastrophic worries, nocturnal checking, panic-like episodes  
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by rumination  
- Feeling “drowning” in everyday tasks; psychomotor fatigue  
- Fleeting passive self-harm thoughts (“what if I just disappeared”) without plan or intent

Observed pattern  
Responses cluster around four domains:  
1. Core depressive symptoms (sadness, loss of pleasure, helplessness)  
2. Heightened anxiety/panic with infant-focused intrusive thoughts  
3. Cognitive distortions of maternal inadequacy/guilt  
4. Functional overload and sleep loss reinforcing distress

Screening significance  
- Meets high-risk profile for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (≥5 DSM-equivalent symptoms, duration implied daily)  
- Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD, panic spectrum) common in postpartum presentations  
- Safety: presence of self-harm ideation, even if fleeting → warrants immediate risk assessment

Risk factors noted  
- Social comparison distress; possible limited support (references to partner only)  
- Sleep deprivation amplifying mood instability  
- No verbalized protective factors/plans against self-harm

Next steps (screening only)  
Recommend urgent clinician-administered Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and standardized suicide-risk interview; consider expedited referral for perinatal mental-health evaluation and support resources.
